skills.trigger: When evaluating a frontal chest X-ray showing left superior mediastinal widening and mild cardiomegaly in a patient with unexplained hypoxaemia or dyspnoea.
steps: Identify the specific location of mediastinal widening: confirm it is localized to the left superior mediastinum (often appearing as a vertical density parallel to the aortic knob) rather than a diffuse mass or right-sided deviation.
Assess the lung fields for signs of pulmonary congestion or edema; note if they are clear despite the presence of cardiac silhouette enlargement.

Correlate the anatomical finding (widened left superior mediastinum) with the physiological symptom (hypoxaemia) by considering a Persistent Left Superior Vena Cava (PLSVC) draining into the left atrium.

Distinguish this from left heart failure (which would typically show pulmonary venous congestion) or compressive masses (which would not inherently cause shunting/hypoxaemia without airway compromise).

skills.trigger: When assessing the superior mediastinum on a PA chest radiograph to differentiate vascular anomalies from pathological masses.
steps: Trace the contour of the left superior mediastinum looking for a smooth, tubular, or convex opacity extending inferiorly from the level of the aortic arch.

Compare the density and margins of the widening to typical lymphadenopathy or tumors; vascular structures like a PLSVC often maintain smooth borders and follow the expected course of the venous system.

Check for associated cardiac findings such as mild left ventricular enlargement or prominence of the coronary sinus region, which supports a congenital venous anomaly over an acquired neoplastic process.
